title: Matplotlib
description: Build charts that make an argument — and label them so nobody has to ask.

lessons.title: Change over time
lessons.lead: Every chart you draw here is rendered under the output panel. Matplotlib loads on the first run — give it a few seconds.

tasks.title: Actual against target
tasks.brief: Draw both series as lines on one axes, label everything, and print the labels back to prove they are set.
steps: Start from `fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.5))`
Plot `sales` with a marker, and `target` dashed and grey
Give both a `label=` so the legend has something to show
Title it `Monthly sales vs target, 2026`, with axes `Month` and `Sales (units)`
starter: # draw both lines, set the title and both axis labels, add a legend
tasks.hint: `ax.plot(months, target, linestyle="--", color="gray", label="Target")` gives the reference line its own look.
tasks.explain: `fig` is the canvas and `ax` is the one plotting area on it. Learning this form now is what makes the two-chart figure in the last lesson straightforward.

tasks.title: Point at the peak
tasks.brief: Find the best month, annotate it on the chart, and print which month it was.
steps: `np.argmax(sales)` gives the position of the highest value
Use that position to look up the month name
Annotate the point with `ax.annotate(text, xy=(month, value), xytext=(...), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->"))`
starter: ax.set_title("Sales grew 58% between January and May")
# find the best month, annotate it, then print: peak May 190
tasks.hint: `int(np.argmax(sales))` gives a plain integer you can use as a list index.
solution: ax.set_title("Sales grew 58% between January and May")
tasks.explain: The title states the finding rather than naming the columns, and the annotation points at the single thing the reader should take away.

lessons.title: Comparing categories
lessons.lead: Bars start at zero and are sorted by value, unless their order carries meaning of its own.

tasks.title: A sorted horizontal bar chart
tasks.brief: Sort the classes by size, draw them as horizontal bars, and print the order you drew them in.
steps: Sort the dictionary items by their value, smallest first
`ax.barh(labels, values)` draws horizontally
Print the sorted labels, then the sorted values
starter: # 1. sort the items by count, smallest first
# 2. draw a horizontal bar chart with a title and an x label
# 3. print the labels, then the values
tasks.hint: `sorted(counts.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1])` gives the pairs in size order.
solution: ax.set_title("Class C has the most students")
tasks.explain: Sorting smallest first puts the longest bar at the top once matplotlib draws the first category at the bottom — which is the order a reader expects.

tasks.title: Label the bars, drop the box
tasks.brief: Write each value at the end of its bar and hide the top and right spines, then print which spines are still visible.
steps: Loop with `enumerate(values)` and call `ax.text(value + 0.3, i, str(value), va="center")`
`ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)` hides two at once
Print the visible spine names as a list
starter: # 1. write each value at the end of its bar
# 2. hide the top and right spines
# 3. print the spines that are still visible
tasks.hint: `[side for side in ["left", "right", "top", "bottom"] if ax.spines[side].get_visible()]` builds the list to print.
tasks.explain: With a handful of bars, a value at the end of each one beats a grid — the reader gets the exact number without tracing a line across the chart.

lessons.title: Relationships and distributions
lessons.lead: One chart for how two numbers move together, one for how a single number is spread out.

tasks.title: Hours against score
tasks.brief: Draw the scatter plot and print the correlation between the two columns, rounded to two places.
steps: `ax.scatter(x, y, alpha=0.6, s=40, edgecolor="white")`
`np.corrcoef(x, y)[0, 1]` is the correlation
Label both axes — a scatter with bare numbers says nothing
starter: # 1. draw the scatter plot with a title and both axis labels
tasks.hint: `round(float(np.corrcoef(hours, score)[0, 1]), 2)` gives a plain number to print.
tasks.explain: A correlation of 0.91 is strong, but the scatter is what tells you whether it is a straight line, a curve, or two clusters pretending to be a trend.

tasks.title: The shape of the scores
tasks.brief: Draw a histogram with a dashed line at the mean, then print the number of bins and the mean.
steps: `ax.hist(scores, bins=8, edgecolor="white")`
`ax.axvline(mean, color="#E8A93B", linestyle="--", linewidth=2, label="Mean")`
Print the bin count, then the mean rounded to two places
starter: # 1. draw a histogram of 8 bins, with a title and both axis labels
# 2. add a dashed line at the mean, and a legend
tasks.hint: The mean is `sum(scores) / len(scores)` — no library needed.
tasks.explain: Change `bins` to 4 and then to 20 and run it again. The data never moved, but the story the chart tells did — which is why the bin count is a decision, not a default.

lessons.title: Finishing a figure
lessons.lead: The last few lines are what turn a plot into something you can put in front of someone.

tasks.title: Rotate, grid, and source
tasks.brief: Rotate the crowded x labels, add a faint grid behind the bars, and print the rotation you applied.
steps: `ax.tick_params(axis="x", rotation=45)` rotates the tick labels
`ax.grid(axis="y", alpha=0.3, linestyle="--")` then `ax.set_axisbelow(True)`
Add the source with `fig.text(0.01, 0.01, "Source: school records, 2026", fontsize=8, color="gray")`
Print the rotation of the first x tick label
starter: ax.set_title("Phnom Penh has twice the enrolment of anywhere else")
# 1. rotate the x tick labels by 45 degrees
# 2. add a faint dashed grid on the y axis, behind the bars
# 3. add the source line to the figure
tasks.hint: `ax.get_xticklabels()[0].get_rotation()` reads the rotation back — wrap it in `int()` to print it cleanly.
solution: ax.set_title("Phnom Penh has twice the enrolment of anywhere else")
tasks.explain: `set_axisbelow(True)` is the difference between a grid that helps and a grid drawn on top of your bars.

tasks.title: Two charts, one figure
tasks.brief: Put the distribution and the relationship side by side, title each one, and print both titles.
steps: `fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.5))` returns an array of axes
Draw the histogram on `axes[0]` and the scatter on `axes[1]`
Print how many axes the figure has, then each title
starter: # 1. one figure, two axes side by side
# 2. histogram of scores on the left, scatter of hours vs sample on the right
# 3. print: 2 axes  then each title on its own line
tasks.hint: `axes[0].set_title("Score distribution")` and `axes[1].set_title("Hours vs score")` — then read them back with `get_title()`.
tasks.explain: `subplots(rows, cols)` hands back an array of axes, and every axes carries its own title, labels, and grid. This is the payoff for using the `fig, ax` form from the very first task.
